title: Welcome to the BMS Blog
author: Editorial Desk
summary: What this blog is for, how often it appears, and what you will find in it.
body:
This blog is a new corner of the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh website. Every Sunday morning it carries one article for karyakartas, workers, students of labour questions and anyone who wants to understand how India's largest national trade union centre thinks, speaks and acts. Before the weekly articles begin, it is worth saying plainly what the blog is for, what it will cover, and what kind of organisation stands behind it.

## Why a blog, and why now

Labour questions in India are often discussed in slogans or in legal jargon, and ordinary workers are left out of both. A worker in a factory, a mine, a bank, a construction site or a village anganwadi centre rarely gets a plain explanation of the law that governs their job, or of the reasons behind a union's demand. A karyakarta who has to explain a Labour Code to a meeting of fifty people needs the same thing: a clear, accurate, readable account that can be checked.

The blog tries to supply that. Each post takes one subject, explains what it is, gives dates and numbers where they are available, says why it matters to workers, and then says what BMS's position is. The aim is not to win arguments but to give readers enough background to form their own view and to take part in discussions with confidence.

## A very short introduction to BMS

The Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh was founded on **23 July 1955** at Bhopal, under the guidance of Dattopant Thengadi. The date is the birth anniversary of Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak. BMS's own account stresses that it did not break away from an older union: when it began, it had no union, no members, no activists, no office and no funds. Everything that exists today was built from that starting point, which is a theme this blog will return to in the next post.

BMS describes itself as nationalist and non-political, meaning that it is not tied to any political party. It draws on Bharatiya culture and on the idea of Integral Humanism, and it does not accept the theory of class struggle. Its stated fight is against injustice and exploitation rather than against any class of people. It treats strikes as a last resort, to be used only after talks, negotiation and arbitration have failed, and it opposes violence.

On size, BMS's website reports affiliated unions in all 44 industries classified by the Ministry of Labour and nearly one crore members, with more than 5,000 affiliated unions. These are self-reported figures. Government membership verification exercises have also been held over the years, and a later post will look at what they showed. Whatever the exact number at any moment, BMS is represented on many national bodies, including the Indian Labour Conference, the Standing Labour Committee, the ESI and EPF bodies, the National Productivity Council and the National Safety Council, and it leads the Indian workers' delegation at International Labour Organization conferences.

## What you will find here

- **Labour law in plain words:** the four Labour Codes, wages, social security, safety and industrial relations, along with the constitutional background that sits behind them.
- **The world of work beyond India:** the International Labour Organization, the BRICS Trade Union Forum and BMS's international engagements.
- **People and ideas:** the life of founder Dattopant Thengadi, the philosophy summed up in *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit*, the three-line motto, and what leaders have said about the movement.
- **Those who are often left out:** unorganised workers, gig and platform workers, and the millions of Anganwadi, ASHA and mid-day meal workers who carry out public schemes without being recognised as workers.
- **Union stories:** how BMS federations in railways, defence, banks, construction, mines and other sectors go about their work.

Each category has its own tag, so a reader who cares only about labour law, or only about history, can follow just that thread.

## Words and symbols you will meet

New readers will notice a few phrases again and again. The motto reads "Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation", and its Hindi form is *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Shramik hit*. "Bharat Mata Ki Jai" is presented in BMS material as a slogan the organisation brought into the labour movement, and "Workers Unite the World" was adopted as an answer to the older slogan "Workers of the World Unite". Another line often heard at BMS gatherings translates roughly as: work in the country's interest and take full wages for the work.

The BMS symbol combines an industrial wheel, a plough-like motif for agriculture and a human fist for the unity of workers, and BMS observes Vishwakarma Day as National Labour Day. Several of these points will get a post of their own. For now it is enough to know that they are part of the organisation's identity and that the blog will explain each one rather than assume prior knowledge.

## How we write

Posts are written from public sources: the BMS website, the Ministry of Labour and Employment, the International Labour Organization, the text of the Constitution and the Acts of Parliament, and the press. Where a post describes a BMS position, it says that this is BMS's position, so that readers can tell the difference between a description of the law and a statement of what the union wants. Where a source is a publication close to the movement, that is worth bearing in mind, and the posts try to say so.

Figures and dates are cited at the end of each post under "Sources and further reading", so that anyone can follow the link and check. We try to paraphrase rather than quote, to keep the tone factual and calm, and to avoid attacks on any party or person. Labour questions are serious enough without them. If we do not know something, or if sources disagree, the post will say so rather than guess.

If you spot an error, please tell the web team so that it can be corrected. Corrections are part of how a record stays honest.

## A note on dates

The first hundred posts of this blog cover the period from December 2024 to November 2026. They were prepared together and are dated by Sunday, so that the archive reads as a continuous weekly record. From here on, a new post is published every Sunday at 7:00 am.

## What to do next

Read the posts in order if you are new to BMS: the founding at Bhopal, the thinking behind the motto, the life of Thengadi, and then the legal and policy posts. Read them out of order if you only need one subject. Share them with colleagues, bring them to union meetings, and, above all, write to us with the questions you would like answered. A blog for workers is only useful if it answers what workers actually ask.
